thread.title: Roku Stock Rises On Ad-Supported Streaming Video

author: PATRICK SEITZ
title: Roku Stock Rises On Ad-Supported Streaming Video
text:
Roku ( ROKU ) provides a popular platform for viewing subscription video-on-demand services like Netflix ( NFLX ), but increasingly its users are watching free, advertiser-supported streaming channels, the company said late Wednesday.
X That trend helped the Los Gatos, Calif.-based company beat Wall Street's sales and earnings targets for the March quarter. It also guided higher for the current quarter and full year.
But Roku shares dipped 1.7% to close at 35.46 on the stock market today . The company went public at 14 on Sept. 28. It reached an all-time high of 58.80 on Dec. 19.
Roku ended the quarter with 20.8 million active accounts, up 1.5 million from the December quarter. Streaming hours on the platform increased 56% year over year to 5.1 billion hours, with the fastest growth coming from ad-supported content.

Please contact customer service CLOSE The company is focused on growth and with a goal this year of running the business at or near break-even.
Roku lost an adjusted 7 cents a share in the first quarter as sales rose 36% year over year to $136.6 million. Analysts expected the company to lose 16 cents a share on sales of $128 million, according to Zacks Investment Research.
Smart TV Share Growing Roku licenses a smart-TV operating system to consumer electronics firms. It also makes its own set-top boxes and TV dongles for accessing internet television services.
The company faces competition from rival streaming devices from Amazon.com ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ) and others, as well as TV manufacturers opting for alternative operating systems.
Roku monetizes its platform and user base mostly through advertising sales. It also gets a share of sales from pay-per-view and subscription video-on-demand services.
One in four smart TVs sold in the U.S. last quarter were Roku TVs. That's up from one in five in 2017. Half of Roku's new accounts in the first quarter came from licensed sources, primarily Roku TVs.
Most of Roku's users are in the U.S., but the company operates in 23 countries internationally, Roku Chief Financial Officer Steve Louden told Investor's Business Daily.
"We feel like we're in the early days of streaming taking off in the U.S. and certainly internationally, so there's a big opportunity ahead," he said. More than 40% of the content on Roku has ads, Louden said.
Roku Channel On More Devices Roku launched its own advertiser-supported streaming channel, the Roku Channel, eight months ago. It is now one of the top 15 channels on Roku devices, based on hours streamed.
The company is working to get the Roku Channel on non-Roku devices, starting with Samsung TVs this summer.
Roku believes there's a big opportunity to sell advertising for over-the-top internet television as cord-cutting and the shift to streaming video continue.
"Today, roughly 10% of all adults between 18 and 34 can only be reached on TV on the Roku platform in the living room," Roku executives said in a letter to shareholders Wednesday. "We expect that number to grow, which should make our platform an even more important way for brands to engage TV viewers."
William Blair analyst Ralph Schackart reiterated his outperform rating on Roku stock on Thursday.
"As the traditional-TV ad market transitions in favor of OTT (over-the-top) and streamed video, we believe Roku is well positioned to take advantage," he said in a report.
KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst Evan Wingren maintained his overweight rating on Roku, but raised his price target to 44 from 42.
"The shift to streaming video, smart-TV share gains, and early results from the Roku Channel are translating into platform growth above expectations, and the outlook still sets up conservatively from here," Wingren said in a report. "Long term, we see proof points that Roku's competitive position in streaming is strengthening."
